facts.title: Rock and Roll Peak (1956)
facts.body: The first cycle of rock and roll, beginning in 1951, peaked with Elvis Presley in 1956, marking a significant high point for the genre. "It peaked with Elvis in 1956."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Pioneering Music Merchandise (1956)
facts.body: Elvis Presley was the first artist to have a comprehensive merchandising deal, initiated by his manager Colonel Tom Parker and Hank Saperstein of Special Products Inc. This deal, involving over 30 different items from T-shirts to sneakers, generated $22 million in sales within six months in 1956, effectively launching the modern music merchandising industry. "There were at least 30 different items ranking from T-shirts to sneakers to belts."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rock Explainer
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut – First Appearance (September 9, 1956)
facts.body: Elvis Presley made his initial appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" on September 9, 1956. This first performance occurred without any reported controversy or incident. "The first appearance on September 9th went off just fine."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Ed Sullivan Show – Second Appearance Controversy (October 28, 1956)
facts.body: Elvis's second appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" on October 28, 1956, generated significant public outrage, primarily due to his "swiveling hips." CBS reportedly received thousands of complaints, largely from religious groups, who objected to his "blatant sexual moves." "But the second, airing on October 28th, caused clutching of pearls because of Elvis's swibbling hips. CBS reportedly received thousands of outraged phone calls and letters, many from religious groups complaining about Elvis's blatant sexual moves."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Legend's Birth Date (September 9, 1956)
facts.body: The legend of Elvis Presley is often considered to have truly begun on September 9, 1956, marking a pivotal day in his career. This specific date is referred to as the day "the greatest myth in music history" was built. "el 9 de septiembre de 1956 fue prácticamente de manera un ánime el día que nací la leyenda."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Transition to RCA (1956)
facts.body: In 1956, Elvis Presley departed from Sun Records, the smaller record label that had initially discovered him, to sign with RCA. At the time, RCA was recognized as the largest record company in the world. "el BISI había dejado a San Records que era esa pequeña discográfica que había descubierto y se había ido a la RCA que era la discográfica más grande del mundo de aquellas."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: First Ed Sullivan Appearance (September 9, 1956)
facts.body: Elvis Presley made his inaugural performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on September 9, 1956. During this appearance, he sang three songs, and as was becoming common at his concerts, "panic broke out" among the audience. "El primero fue el 9 de septiembre de 1956."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Record-Breaking Ed Sullivan Broadcast (1956)
facts.body: Following a highly complex production process, the program featuring Elvis Presley was broadcast, achieving an audience of over six million people and an 82% share. This was considered "crazy" for the era and made it the most-watched program of the entire 'tibuenta' decade (referring to the 1950s). "acabó teniendo más de seis millones de personas de audiencia, en aquella época era una locura, fue 82% de cierta. El programa más visto de toda la década de los tibuenta."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Memphis Concerts (September 1956)
facts.body: A few days after his impactful Ed Sullivan appearance, still in September 1956, Elvis Presley performed two "very big concerts" in "la mamá" (Memphis). These events further amplified his burgeoning legend. "pocos días después, todavía en septiembre de 1956 vinieron esos dos grandísimos conciertos que hizo en la mamá que todavía incrementaron más la leyenda."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: Second Ed Sullivan Appearance & Interview (October 1956)
facts.body: In October, a few days after the Memphis concerts, Elvis Presley returned for the second of his three contracted programs with Ed Sullivan. By this point, Sullivan himself personally interviewed Elvis, recognizing him as the undisputed star of the moment. "en octubre, Elvis iba al segundo de los tres programas que había fermado con el sul-bank y ya el sul-bank iba personalmente a entrevistar a Elvis porque era la estrella del momento."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito
facts.name: Elvis Presley

facts.title: 21st Birthday Session (1956)
facts.body: Elvis entered the studio on January 10th, 1956, two days after his 21st birthday, under immense pressure to record something extraordinary for RCA. "When Elvis went into the studio on January 10th, 1956, two days after his 21st birthday, the pressure was on him to record something very special indeed."

facts.title: Origin of the Term "Rock and Roll" – Moondog Lawsuit Forces Alan Freed to Coin the Phrase (1956)
facts.body: DJ Alan Freed popularized R&B music to white audiences using the name "Moondog" (borrowed without permission from blind musician Lewis Harden, who had used it since 1947) for his radio show and concerts. In 1956, Harden sued Freed for trademark infringement and won. Forced to abandon the name, Freed adopted "Rock and Roll" — drawn from African-American slang for sex, as heard in the 1951 song "60 Minute Man" — using it as a "secret code" for teenagers. "Freed adopted 'Rock and Roll' from African-American slang for sex, using it as a 'secret code' for teenagers."

facts.title: First Cycle Peak and Decline (1956-1960s)
facts.body: The first cycle peaked with Elvis in 1956 but began its decline on March 2, 1958, with Elvis's army enlistment. This period, lasting into the 1960s, saw rock declared a "fad" by record executives. "It peaked with Elvis in 1956. The day new Ma began on March 2nd of 1958."

facts.body: In 1956, the *Daily Mirror* declared rock and roll to be "out of date" and "old-fashioned," anticipating that "think-a-fold music" (skiffle) would become the new craze. This premature declaration of its demise reflected a common pattern of older generations dismissing new musical trends. "Rock and roll is out of date, old-fashioned."

facts.body: In 1956, record labels struggled to understand how to market and manage white rock and roll acts for the teenage crowd, beyond established stars like Bill Haley and Elvis Presley or packaged Sun Records artists. facts.title: Image Shift to Black Man with Piano (Late 1956)
facts.body: In late 1956, the default image for a rock and roll star was a black man with a piano, primarily due to the immense record sales and popularity of artists like Fats Domino, a notable contrast to the later "white man with guitar" image. "But in late 1956 that default image was a black man with a piano and the black man with a piano who was selling the most records by far was Fat Stomano."

facts.title: Revolutionary Context (1956)
facts.body: Rock and roll was seen as profoundly revolutionary in 1956, largely because it facilitated racial integration through music, with white teenagers actively listening to and imitating black musicians at a critical juncture in the civil rights struggle. "This, as much as anything musical, is the context you need to understand why rock and roll was seen as so revolutionary in 1956 in particular."

facts.title: Origins of the Word "Psychedelic" – Coined 1956 by Psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond; Means "Soul-Revealing" in Greek
facts.body: The word "psychedelic" was coined in 1956 by British psychiatrist Humphrey Osmond, who was studying pharmaceuticals including LSD (Lysergic Acid Diethylamide, first synthesized from the ergot fungus by Swiss scientist Albert Hofmann in 1943 and marketed commercially for a period under the brand name Delysid). The CIA also studied LSD for potential use in interrogation, chemical warfare, and mind control. As the drugs spread recreationally, artists took notice and the word became an adjective for anything mind-expanding. "Psychedelic means soul revealing in Greek."

facts.body: Despite Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill" being listed among Billboard's top 30 country sellers for the year, it never appeared on the top 100 country charts in 1956, illustrating strict genre segregation. facts.title: Conflicting Accounts of Million Dollar Quartet Participation (1956)
facts.body: Accounts vary widely regarding Johnny Cash's involvement in the legendary Million Dollar Quartet session on December 4, 1956. Cash himself claimed he was the first to arrive and the last to leave, watching his friends record and staying for the entire jam session. Other versions suggest he arrived mid-session to collect a royalty check, sang a few songs off-tape, and then left for Christmas shopping. Yet another account implies Sam Phillips, seeking publicity for Sun Records' biggest act, called Cash, along with journalists and photographers, implying Cash only appeared for a photo opportunity before departing. "Every single account of what became known as the million dollar quartet session disagrees as to how much, ever at all, Johnny Cash participated in the proceedings."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins
facts.name: Johnny Cash

facts.title: Singing Style on Million Dollar Quartet Tapes (1956)
facts.body: On the Million Dollar Quartet jam session tapes, which were recorded on a single microphone and released in the 1980s, Johnny Cash is difficult to hear. He claimed he was positioned furthest from the microphone and sang in a higher register than usual to match the keys comfortable for the other three musicians (Elvis Presley, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Carl Perkins). "Cash always said that he was there, just the furthest from the microphone, and that he was singing in a higher register than normal, because he was trying to sing in the keys that were comfortable for the other three."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins
facts.name: Johnny Cash

facts.body: After December 4, 1956, Johnny Cash, along with Carl Perkins, increasingly moved towards country music and away from rockabilly. "They both moved increasingly towards country music, and away from rockabilly."

facts.title: Discovery and Early Recordings (1956)
facts.body: Jerry Lee Lewis was discovered by Sam Phillips' assistant, Cowboy Jack Clement, in November 1956. He cut his first record for Sun Records a couple of weeks before the December 4, 1956 session, and that first record was released three days prior to that session. "Jerry Lee Lewis was a new piano player, who had been discovered by Sam Phillips as assistant, Cowboy Jack Clement, the previous month."

facts.title: Session Musician for Christmas Presents (1956)
facts.body: On December 4, 1956, Jerry Lee Lewis participated in Carl Perkins' recording session for "Matchbox" not as a primary performer, but as a session musician. His motivation was to earn enough money to buy Christmas presents for his parents. "but he was just working as a session musician, trying to earn enough money to buy his parents some Christmas presents, by sitting in on the session."

facts.title: Failed Louisiana Hayride Attempt (1956)
facts.body: Elvis had assured Buddy Holly that the Louisiana Hayride would feature him based on his recommendation. However, when Holly and Sonny Curtis drove to Shreveport, the radio station informed them that Elvis did not control their bookings, forcing them to return to Texas without performing. "Elvis had told him that the Louisiana Hayride would definitely have him on at Elvis's recommendation, but when he and Sonny Curtis drove to Shreveport, the radio station told him that it wasn't up to Elvis who got on their show and who didn't."

facts.title: Decca Records Misspells Name (1956)
facts.body: When signing his paperwork for Decca Records, Charles Holley (H-O-L-L-E-Y) discovered his name was misspelled as H-O-L-L-Y. Told they needed the document back quickly, he signed it, and from then on, he was known as Buddy Holly, without the 'e'. "When the paperwork for it came through for Buddy to sign, he discovered that they'd miss spelled his name."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Buddy Holly

facts.title: Decca's Disillusionment (1956)
facts.body: Throughout 1956, Decca Records grew increasingly disillusioned with Buddy Holly's lack of commercial success, despite numerous recordings. Paul Cohen, the executive who signed Holly, was known to tell friends that Buddy Holly was "the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with." "Decker became ever more disillusioned with Holly, while Paul Cohen, the executive at Decker who had signed Holly, at one point was telling his friends, Buddy Holly is the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Buddy Holly

facts.title: End of 1956 Career Stagnation
facts.body: As 1956 drew to a close, Buddy Holly found himself in a difficult position: without his long-time guitarist Sonny Curtis, signed to a record company that did not know how to promote him, and failing to realize his musical ambitions despite constant recording. "So as 1956 drew to a close, Buddy Holly was without his long-time guitarist, signed to a record company that didn't know what to do with him, and failing to realise his musical ambitions."

facts.title: Dominant Black Rock & Roll Star (1956)
facts.body: By late 1956, after many white rockabilly acts had faded from the US charts, Fats Domino, alongside Little Richard and Chuck Berry, stood as one of the few black R&B stars consistently delivering rock and roll hits. At this time, the default image for a rock and roll star was a black man with a piano, and Domino was by far the biggest record seller in this category. "But in late 1956 that default image was a black man with a piano and the black man with a piano who was selling the most records by far was Fat Stomano."

facts.title: Racial Context of 1956
facts.body: Fats Domino's remarkable commercial success in 1956 occurred against a backdrop of intense racial tension and the burgeoning Civil Rights Movement. Events like the murder of Emmett Till, Rosa Parks' defiance, and escalating white supremacist violence highlighted the societal conflict, making rock and roll's appeal to white teenagers listening to black musicians a revolutionary force. "This, as much as anything musical, is the context you need to understand why rock and roll was seen as so revolutionary in 1956 in particular."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Las Vegas Residency Incident (1956)
facts.body: Gene Vincent and The Blue Caps secured a lucrative Las Vegas residency, earning $3,000 a week, a "staggering sum" for 1956. However, when manager Tex Davis relayed the casino owner's demand (backed by the mafia) for Vincent to tone down his act, Vincent reacted defiantly. He went on stage, performed only one song, then spotted Davis in the crowd, gave him "the finger," and walked off, leaving his band to finish the show without him. This act of insubordination led to the residency's abrupt cancellation and Davis terminating his management contract. "Instead, Jean went on stage, sang one song, found Tex Davis in the crowd, caught his eye, flipped him off, and walked off stage, leaving the band to do the rest of the show without him."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: End of First Wave Rockabilly Success (1956)

facts.title: Mistakenly Predicted as New Craze (1956)
facts.body: In 1956, the *Daily Mirror* newspaper mistakenly predicted that "think-a-fold music" (skiffle) would be the new coming craze, supplanting rock and roll, which they declared "out of date, old-fashioned." They observed London's espresso bars turning into modern versions of old-time music halls, indicating a shift they believed would lead to skiffle's dominance. "Think-a-fold music is the new coming craze?"

facts.body: The A-side of Elvis's biggest double-sided hit, definitely chosen by Elvis, and written by Otis Blackwell (credited to Blackwell and Presley due to Colonel Parker's insistence). This song showed a new "lightness of touch" in Elvis's performance, as he was finally in control of the studio sound. It took 28 takes, but resulted in a "light, fluffy sound" where Elvis sounded playful. It was the song that convinced several detractors, including Sam Phillips, of Elvis's ability to make good records away from Sun. It reached number 1 on the charts, then number 2, and along with "Hound Dog," spent 11 weeks at the top. "Elvis's version showed a lightness of touch that had been absent on his earlier RCA records."

facts.body: Chosen by Elvis for his first RCA session, this song was initially conceived by Tommy Durden (inspired by a newspaper story about a man, possibly Alvin Crowley, who died by suicide or was shot during a robbery), with Mae Axton contributing the iconic "heartbreak hotel" phrase. Glenn Reeves helped finish it and recorded the demo but refused credit. Elvis instantly loved the song, which reminded him of Roy Brown's "Hard-Luck Blues," and Mae Axton insisted it would be his first million-seller. Despite criticisms about its reverb sound compared to Sun Records' slapback, it became a smash hit, reaching number one on the Pop and Country charts and the top five in R&B, marking his transformation into "the King of Rock and Roll." "He instantly fell in love with the song, which reminded the young blues lover of Roy Brown's hard-look blues."

It took 31 takes to record and, combined with "Don't Be Cruel," spent 11 weeks at the top of the charts, reaching number 2 before swapping with "Don't Be Cruel" to hit number 1. "These days, their cover version of Big Mama Thunton's Hound Dog is the better known of the two sides they cut that day, but while that's an excellent track, and one that bears almost no relation to Thunton's original."

facts.body: A major hit for Elvis Presley in 1956, "Hound Dog" was one of the prominent rock and roll songs of the year, though its worldwide chart positions were ultimately surpassed by Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill." "Worldwide, Blueberry Hill was the biggest rock and roll hit of 1956, outdoing even Elvis's Hound Dog and Hard Break Hotel in Worldwide Chart positions."

facts.title: Parody and Copyright Precedent (1956)
facts.body: Dickie Goodman was taken to court for copyright infringement for his 1956 novelty song "Flying Saucer," but a judge ruled it was parody and therefore a brand new composition, allowing him to continue having hits using this method until 1975. "Goodman was taken to court for copyright infringement, but he was left off the hook when a judge declared that this was parody and therefore a brand new composition."

facts.body: This song, written by James Brown and Johnny Terry, was based on something Little Richard had scribbled on a napkin, which Brown saw potential in as a title. It fit a specific genre of R&B ballad, influenced by songs like Flow Example Richards' "Directly from My Heart to You," Fay Adams' "Shake a Hand," and The Orioles' version of Big Joe Williams' "Baby Please Don't Go," from which Brown borrowed the backing vocal arrangement. The emotional intensity of Brown's singing on this track was particularly effective, resonating with a type of woman who felt sympathy for him. The song reached number six on the R&B chart and reportedly sold between one and three million copies, though record companies often inflated sales figures at the time. "Bass was absolutely convinced that please, please, please would be a hit and championed the flames in the face of opposition from his boss, Sid Nathan."

facts.title: Band Formation and Name Origin (1956)
facts.body: The Blue Caps were formed by Gene Vincent as his backing band before his Nashville recording session. Their name was derived from the blue hats they wore on stage, which were reportedly inspired by the golf caps frequently worn by President Eisenhower. This inspiration was humorously noted as "not the most rebellious" for a group that became a significant influence on youthful rebellion. "They took the name Blue Caps from the hats they all wore on stage, which were allegedly inspired by the golf caps that President Eisenhower used to wear while playing golf."

facts.body: This song, initially released as the B-side to "Woman Love," became Gene Vincent's most memorable hit of the 1950s. Its title has multiple origin stories, including being inspired by the 1920s vaudeville song "Don't Ring Lulu" (per Donald Graves), a "Little Lulu" comic book (per Tex Davis, who is credited as co-writer but widely believed not to have contributed to the writing), or most likely Helen Humes' song "Be-Baba-Leba," later re-recorded by Lionel Hampton as "Hey Baba Reba." Lyrically, it's described as "absolute nonsense" and "gibberish," but its sound was pivotal, being the "precise midpoint" between Elvis Presley's "Heartbreak Hotel" and Little Richard's "Tutti Frutti," and is said to epitomize 1956. During its recording, drummer Dickie Harrell famously let out a scream mid-song so his mother would know he was on the record, a take that was ultimately used. "Be-Bop-A-Lula is by any standards, a quite astonishing record."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Departure from Buddy Holly (1956)
facts.body: Sonny Curtis stopped working with Buddy Holly towards the end of 1956 because Owen Bradley, Holly's producer at Decca, disliked Curtis's guitar playing and preferred Holly to record with session musicians. Simultaneously, Curtis received an offer to play guitar for Slim Whitman, then the biggest star in country music. "Around this time, Sonny Curtis stopped working with Holly. Owen Bradley didn't like his guitar playing, and wanted Holly to record with the session musicians he used with everyone else, while Curtis got an offer to play guitar for Slim Whitman, who at the time was about the biggest star in country music."

facts.body: This song was recorded by Jerry Lee Lewis almost as a joke during his first solo session for Sun Records, having also played it on his audition tape. facts.title: Criticism of "That'll Be the Day" (1956)
facts.body: Owen Bradley famously described the first, unreleased Decca recording of "That'll Be the Day" as "the worst song I've ever heard," primarily due to Buddy Holly singing out of his normal range following Webb Pierce's advice. "One of the songs that he recorded during that time, but which wasn't released, was one that Owen Bradley described as the worst song I've ever heard."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets
facts.name: Owen Bradley

facts.title: Disapproval of Sonny Curtis's Playing (1956)
facts.body: Owen Bradley disliked Sonny Curtis's guitar playing and preferred Buddy Holly to record with his own studio session musicians, contributing to Curtis's departure from Holly's band. "Owen Bradley didn't like his guitar playing, and wanted Holly to record with the session musicians he used with everyone else."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets
facts.name: Owen Bradley

facts.body: This song, a suggestion from Steve Sholes for Elvis's fourth RCA session, proved disastrous as Elvis had no feel for it and struggled to learn it, leading to a session where no usable take was recorded. Steve Sholes had to cobble together a take from two different performances. Despite the recording difficulties, it reached number one on the country chart and number three on the pop charts. "But the session went terribly, because Elvis had no feel for the song at all."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley
facts.name: I Want You, I Need You, I Love You

facts.body: Elvis Presley's cover of this song was performed on the "Stage Show" TV program, notably airing simultaneously with Carl Perkins's own TV debut performing the song on "Ozark Jubilee." Initially, a "gentleman's agreement" prevented its release as a single to avoid competing with Perkins's sales, but it was included on Elvis's first album and an EP. When eventually released as a single later in the year, it reached the top 20 and generated additional royalties for Perkins. Elvis's rendition maintains a consistent 4/4 beat throughout and conveys a strong sense of "urgency," contrasting with Perkins's more rhythmically complex original. "Thresley was on stage show on another network, performing his cover version of it."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.name: Blue Suede Shoes

facts.title: Decline in US Charts (Late 1956)
facts.body: The initial wave of white rockabilly acts that achieved prominence between 1955 and 1956, including artists like Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, and Bill Haley, experienced a significant decline by late 1956, failing to secure further major hits in the US. "The wave of white rock-a-billy acts that had hit throughout 1955 and 56 had all fizzled."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino
facts.name: Rock-a-billy

facts.title: Decca Executive's Disbelief in Holly (1956)
facts.body: Paul Cohen, the executive at Decca who signed Buddy Holly, became thoroughly disillusioned with Holly's lack of success in 1956, reportedly telling friends that Holly was "the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with." "Paul Cohen, the executive at Decker who had signed Holly, at one point was telling his friends, Buddy Holly is the biggest no-talent I have ever worked with."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
facts.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets
facts.name: Paul Cohen

facts.body: Elvis Presley performed "Love Me Tender" as a preview on The Ed Sullivan Show, prior to its official release, which significantly amplified its mystique and anticipation. This performance led to unprecedented demand, with people flocking to record stores for three days straight to reserve their copies, resulting in over one million copies sold before its official release. It became the first—and possibly only—gold record in history to achieve this status prior to hitting the market, with photographs existing of long queues for reservations. "Entre esas canciones que cantaría ese día estaría el Love Me Tender que la había cantado justo como presentación porque la publicaría un poco más tarde y ahí venía a incrementar todavía más el mito."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.body: Originally penned by Dave Bartholomew for Smiley Lewis, Fats Domino's remake of "Blue Monday" became his next major hit after "Blueberry Hill," achieving nearly the same level of success. The song notably featured a distinctive bass line motif frequently used by Bartholomew in his arrangements. "Domino's remake of that song would become his next hit after Blueberry Hill, and almost his biggest success."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.body: This song by Doris Day achieved greater worldwide chart success in 1956 than any rock and roll hit, including Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill" and Elvis Presley's "Hound Dog" and "Heartbreak Hotel." Its popularity underscored the continued appeal of gentler pop music to a significant segment of the record-buying public. "Though none of those songs could beat K-Sirah Srirah by Doris Day."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Advice on Hit Singles (1956)
facts.body: Webb Pierce advised Buddy Holly that the key to having a hit single was to sing in a high voice, influencing Holly's vocal performance on the unreleased first version of "That'll Be the Day." "Buddy had been told by WebPS that the way to have a hit single was to sing in a high voice, and so he sang the song for her out of his normal range."
facts.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

facts.title: Unreleased Decca Song
facts.body: The fourth song recorded at Buddy Holly's first Decca session, intended as an entry in the "Annie series" and written by Luke McDaniel. It was suggested by Jim Denny, but the label seems to have had second thoughts due to its theme, and it was not released as the single. "And the fourth song that buddy recorded at this first Decker session, Midnight Shift, was intended to be another in the Annie series."
